title: Smart offices: A productivity and well-being perspective
central_proposition: Smart offices, as a distinctive type of space, require dedicated research to understand how smart technologies affect employee productivity and well-being, as insights from smart homes or manufacturing are not directly transferable.

concept_definitions.name: Smart technologies
concept_definitions.definition: technologies that are embedded with artificial intelligence... to collect data from the surrounding environment and assist users in day-to-day activities

concept_definitions.name: Smart offices
concept_definitions.definition: Workplaces embedded with smart technologies, distinct from smart homes/cities/manufacturing, with unique implications for productivity and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Digital workplace
concept_definitions.definition: enables any employee to complete a task, share information and work as a member of a team with other employees in the organisation and in any partner organisation on a totally location-independent basis for all the parties concerned

concept_definitions.name: Virtual teams
concept_definitions.definition: a temporary, culturally diverse, geographically dispersed, electronically communicating workgroup

concept_definitions.name: Cyberslacking
concept_definitions.definition: a phenomenon in which employees are distracted by non-work Internet browsing when they should be accomplishing work tasks

argument_structure: The paper first establishes the prevalence and impact of smart technologies in other domains (cities, homes, manufacturing). It then identifies a research gap regarding smart offices, arguing that existing research on other domains is not directly transferable. It conducts a literature review to synthesize existing findings on technology's impact on productivity and well-being in workplaces, categorizing them into themes (ICT system design, virtual teams, social networking, mobile devices/cyberslacking, office environment control, office layout). Finally, it proposes a research agenda to address the identified gaps, focusing on the unique aspects of smart offices.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Smart technologies influence productivity and well-being through: 1) Efficiency gains via automation and enhanced communication. 2) Affordances enabling new possibilities for work visualization, innovation, collaboration, and simulation. 3) Organisational restructuring leading to higher-skilled roles and decentralization. 4) Environmental control optimizing comfort (thermal, lighting) as a prerequisite for performance. 5) Facilitated social interaction and collaboration. 6) Increased flexibility through mobile devices. 7) Positive psychological states such as perceived control, reduced stress from personal chores, and increased commitment to the firm.

findings.antecedent: Smart technologies (e.g., controlling thermal conditions and lighting)
findings.mechanism: By providing environmental comfort, which is a prerequisite for productivity. The paper suggests testing this at an individual level, considering perception of comfort as a better indicator due to adaptability.
findings.quote: There is a need to test the effect of smart technologies (e.g. controlling thermal conditions and lighting) on the wellbeing of employees at an individual level and not just the space itself.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Seppanen & Fisk (2004) for comfort as prerequisite for productivity.

findings.mechanism: Employees' satisfaction is partially dependent on perceived control. Future studies need to examine the moderating effect of perceived control on the relationship between technology use and comfort.
findings.quote: Given that employees' satisfaction is partially dependent on the perceived degree of control over environmental conditions... future studies need to examine the moderating effect that perceived control has on the relationship between technology use and comfort.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fard (2006), Leaman & Bordass (1999) for satisfaction dependent on perceived control.

findings.antecedent: Indoor environment control systems (in shared vs. traditional offices)
findings.mechanism: Comparative approach to investigate how control systems affect wellbeing, considering potential conflicts in open spaces and how power/control negotiation impacts individual and group satisfaction.
findings.quote: There is a need to adopt a comparative approach to investigate how indoor environment control systems affect satisfaction and productivity, by focusing on the wellbeing of employees in shared vs. traditional offices.

findings.antecedent: Immersion enabled by smart technologies (simulating outdoor environment, virtual interaction with pets via smart walls/telecommunication tools)
findings.mechanism: To substitute for the positive effect of nature and live animals on productivity, while eliminating health-related risks.
findings.quote: Therefore, future studies could focus on the question as to whether immersion enabled by smart technologies can have a similar effect on productivity as live pets and plants in offices do.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Barker (2005) et al. for positive effect of outdoor environment/animals.

findings.antecedent: Smart technologies (e.g., smart cameras, wearable smart trackers, integrated with computer dashboards and health surveillance systems)
findings.consequent: Challenges for employees with various physical conditions in the office environment
findings.mechanism: To address challenges related to diversity and inclusion, and empower employees with disabilities and special requirements.
findings.quote: The agenda for future studies could include research that examines how smart technologies... may tackle such challenges and empower employees with various physical conditions in the office environment.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Sumner & Brown (2015) for diversity/inclusion and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Smart technologies (in different settings: formal vs informal, busy vs relaxed; at different times of day: during breaks vs work)
findings.mechanism: To identify how smart technologies can adapt to different work requirements and investigate the relationship with wellbeing and productivity across various contexts.
findings.quote: Future research needs to examine how smart technologies can be used in different settings... and at different times of the day... to investigate the relationship with wellbeing and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Home-based workplaces (controlled and automated by smart technology)
findings.mechanism: To understand the impact of smart home technologies when used for work, given the heightened responsibility of organizations for employee wellbeing and societal impact.
findings.quote: There is a need to examine the effect that home-based workplaces, controlled and automated by smart technology, has on employees' perceived productivity and wellbeing.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Harpaz (2002) for implications of remote workplaces.

findings.antecedent: Physical and monetary inputs invested by the organisation (e.g., employer subsidises smart home installations and office equipment)
findings.mechanism: By fostering a feeling of commitment and obligation to the firm, due to the creation of favourable environmental conditions.
findings.quote: The productivity of employees may also result from a feeling of commitment and obligation to a firm... Therefore, future research could examine the mediating role of perceived commitment, obligation and loyalty to organisations in the relationship between smart technology utilisation in homes and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Factors hindering smart technology adoption (labour force skills, organisational structure readiness, compatibility of existing technological infrastructure)
findings.mechanism: These factors act as barriers or facilitators to smart technology adoption, leading to low implementation.
findings.quote: First, organisations may experience a shortage of the resources required for the successful integration of smart devices. Therefore, future studies may investigate the factors, such as labour force skills, the readiness of organisational structure, the compatibility of existing technological infrastructure with smart devices, which can be barriers to or facilitators of smart technology adoption.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Etro (2009), Marston et al. (2011) for embeddedness of ICT but overlooking smart devices impact.

findings.antecedent: Organisational culture (resistant to changes towards more intelligent buildings), management beliefs (smart technologies pose security, privacy, financial, other threats)
findings.mechanism: Distrust towards technology and resistance to change due to cultural factors and perceived threats hinder adoption.
findings.quote: Second, firms might not be ready to adopt smart technologies due to organisation culture, which may be resistant to any changes towards more intelligent buildings.

findings.antecedent: Smart technologies (remote management of personal chores like house monitoring, pet care)
findings.consequent: Stress and negative emotions (e.g., dissatisfaction, fatigue)
findings.mechanism: By reducing stress and bringing positive emotions (relaxation), smart technologies contribute to psychological wellbeing. Limiting their use in the workplace might increase stress and dissatisfaction.
findings.quote: Smart technologies can help with the remote management of personal chores... which may reduce stress and bring positive emotions... Consequently, it contributes to psychological wellbeing.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kavanaugh et al. (2012), Khan et al. (2014) for mobile technology use and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Digital workplace practice allowing employees to connect to smart home installations (e.g., visual interaction with family, responding to home activity)
findings.consequent: Feeling of guilt due to being distant from family, associated stress
findings.mechanism: By bringing the home and work closer, it mitigates pressure in work-life balance and reduces negative emotions.
findings.quote: A digital workplace practice that allows employees to connect to their smart home installations actively may help bring the two closer together and mitigate some of the pressure in the work-life balance.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Smart technologies (e.g., for thermal and lighting control) will increase employee well-being at an individual level, with perceived comfort being a key indicator.
Perceived control over environmental conditions will moderate the relationship between technology use and comfort in smart offices.
Indoor environment control systems will differentially affect employee satisfaction and productivity in shared versus traditional office layouts, influenced by power and control negotiation.

Smart technologies enabling immersion (e.g., simulating nature or virtual pet interaction) will positively affect productivity, similar to the presence of real nature or animals, but without associated health risks.

Smart technologies (e.g., smart cameras, wearable trackers, health surveillance systems) can effectively address challenges for employees with physical conditions, thereby empowering them in the office environment.
Smart technologies will adapt to different work requirements across various settings (formal/informal, busy/relaxed) and times of day (breaks/work), influencing employee well-being and productivity.
Home-based workplaces, when controlled and automated by smart technology, will positively affect employees' perceived productivity and well-being.
Organisational investment in smart home installations and office equipment will increase employee productivity by fostering a sense of commitment and obligation to the firm.

Labour force skills, organisational structure readiness, and compatibility of existing technological infrastructure will act as barriers or facilitators to the successful integration of smart devices in offices.
Organisational culture (resistance to change) and management's perceived threats (security, privacy, financial) will hinder smart technology adoption.
Smart technologies that enable remote management of personal chores will decrease employee stress and negative emotions, contributing to psychological well-being.
Digital workplace practices allowing employees to connect with smart home installations will reduce feelings of guilt and stress related to work-life balance.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly connects smart office research to existing frameworks from smart cities, smart homes, and smart manufacturing, arguing for distinct considerations.
It draws on concepts like affordances (Zammuto et al., 2007) from cognitive psychology/HCI.
It links environmental comfort to productivity, citing work from thermal comfort and lighting research.
It discusses trust in virtual teams, linking to social psychology.
It discusses cyberslacking, linking to behavioral economics/HCI.
methodological_critiques: Empirical research lacks evidence on the application and outcomes of smart technologies in workplace settings.
Research from other contexts (smart homes, cities, manufacturing) is not directly transferable to smart offices.
The current literature focuses on the role of technology in work processes, disregarding its role in managing workspaces for productivity and employee well-being.
Prior literature focused only on the effect of smart mobile technology utilization on productivity through engagement in work-related and non-work-related activities.
limitations: The paper itself is an opinion paper and proposes a research agenda, so its 'findings' are theoretical propositions for future research, not empirical results.
Acknowledges that existing research from other domains (smart homes, cities, manufacturing) is not directly transferable to smart offices.
Mentions 'low implementation of smart technologies' as a factor hindering research.
